transcript: Submit Puzzle Ideas helps you make your own The Fantastical Logic Grid puzzle, step by step, and send it to the team. This video shows every entry, what it is for, and how it fits into the puzzle the wizard builds. On thelogicgrid.com, choose Submit Puzzle Ideas. A box asks which puzzle you would like to make. Choose The Fantastical Logic Grid. The wizard goes one step at a time. There are 6 steps, and you can jump back to any of them. Everything you type is saved on this device as you go. Leave and come back later, and your draft is waiting. Start over clears it when you want a fresh start.

Watch how it works opens this video and a written guide to every entry. Show help on every field shows what to write, an example, and how each entry is used in your puzzle. Step 1: Your story. Start with the world of your puzzle: its name, the scene and how it ends. Title, which is required. The name of your puzzle. Printed at the top of the puzzle and the PDF, and shown in Saved puzzles and in your credit.

Look. The game theme whose colors, pictures and music suit your story best. Picks the colors, scene pictures and music when your puzzle is played in the game. Opening scene, which is required. Set the scene in two to four sentences: where we are, and what went wrong or what needs working out. Becomes the first paragraphs of the puzzle. The wizard adds who is in it, what to match and the question at the end. Ending. What happens once the puzzle is solved. Leave it empty and the wizard writes one from the answer. Shown when the puzzle is solved, and printed on the answer key.

Tone. The feel of your story. Helps the team place your puzzle and choose its music. It does not change the clues. Difficulty, which is required. How hard the puzzle should be. Bigger grids are harder at every level. Sets which kinds of clues the wizard may use and how much reasoning each step needs. Step 2: Who is in it. The people (or animals, robots…) your players match up. They make the first column of the grid.

Who they are, which is required. One word for the people in your story, and the word for more than one. The heading of the grid's first column, and the word the clues and questions use ("Which guest…?"). Names, which is required. 3 to 8 different names. Every list you add needs one item for each name. The first column of the grid. The number of names sets the size of the grid: 4 names make a 4 by 4 grid for each list. Step 3: What they are matched with. Two to four lists of things to match. Each list becomes a column of the grid.

Lists to match, which is required. Give each list a name and its items, separated by commas. Use exactly one item for each name. Each list becomes a column of the grid, and the wizard writes clues about it. Ordered lists (times, prices, ages) also get clues like "arrived earlier than". Step 4: The answer. Decide who has what. The wizard writes clues that lead to exactly this answer, and only this one. Who decides the answer?. Choose the answer yourself, or let the wizard pick one. The clues are written to lead to this answer and no other, so every player reaches the same solution.

Answer key. For each name, pick their item in every list. Each item can go to one name only. Printed on the answer key page. The wizard checks it, then writes clues that prove it step by step. Step 5: Pictures and sounds. Optional: add your own pictures and sounds for your puzzle. Pictures and sounds. Up to 3 pictures and 2 sounds that you made yourself. For each one, say what it is for, whether we may use it, and how to credit you. The team can use them with your puzzle in the game: a cover or scene picture, a sound when it is solved, or background music.

At the bottom of every step, your storyline is shown live: the puzzle's words as players will read them. It is read only, and it updates as you type in the fields above. Step 6: Credit and permission. How you would like to be credited, and your permission to use your puzzle. Author credit. The name shown in the author credits of your puzzle. Printed on your puzzle and shown in the game's credits if it is published.

Permission, which is required. Tick the box to say you made the puzzle yourself, and that the team may use and publish it with the credit you chose. We can only save and publish your puzzle with your permission. Check my puzzle opens a new page. The box at the top says whether your puzzle is ready: it must have exactly one answer that players can reason out. Anything missing or wrong is listed, with a link straight to the field, and suggestions to make it better. Every entry is here in one editor, so you can fix or change anything. Each change is checked again straight away, so you always know whether the puzzle is still valid.

When you are happy, press Build my puzzle. Download the PDF to keep or share it, or print it straight away. It has your puzzle and its answer key. Your puzzle is also saved to your Saved puzzles, so you can play it in the game, and a copy goes to the team, who may publish it with your credit. Want to change something? Make changes takes you back to the editor, with suggestions shown and the one-answer check, then build it again. Answer the questions, check and fix, then build, print and play. Have fun making puzzles!
